# ferrolink

**Fast, parallel link checker for static HTML builds.**

[![Powered by Sebastian Software](https://img.shields.io/badge/Powered_by-Sebastian_Software-005164?style=flat)](https://oss.sebastian-software.com) [![CI](https://github.com/sebastian-software/ferrolink/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/sebastian-software/ferrolink/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![MSRV](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.96%2B-orange.svg)](Cargo.toml)

ferrolink reads the output directory of a static site build and checks that
every link, asset reference, and `#fragment` points at something the build
contains. It parses every page in parallel, resolves references the way a
browser does, and maps URLs onto files the way static hosts do. It needs no
server and no network. The Rust CLI also audits sitemaps, canonicals,
`noindex` directives, and Googlebot crawl rules before deployment.

It was built to gate releases and deployments of
[Ardo](https://github.com/sebastian-software/ardo) documentation sites, and
works on the output of any static site generator. It ships as a command-line
tool on crates.io and as an npm package with prebuilt native binaries, a
JavaScript API, and a Vite plugin.

```console
$ ferrolink check docs/build/pages --exclude 'v[345]/**'
v6/guide/component-playground/index.html
  line 17    broken link     /v6/storybook

1 issue in 1 file · 318 pages · 10845 internal links checked · 482 external not checked · 24 ms
```

[Website and getting started](https://sebastian-software.github.io/ferrolink/) ·
[Node.js and Vite reference](https://sebastian-software.github.io/ferrolink/reference/node/)

## What it checks

- **Links and assets**: `a`, `area`, and `link` `href`; `script`, `img`,
  `source`, `video`, `audio`, `track`, `iframe`, and `embed` `src`; `srcset`
  candidates on `img` and `source`; `imagesrcset` candidates on image
  preloads; `video` `poster`; `object` `data`; SVG `use` and `image`; `meta`
  refresh targets; `og:image`, `og:url`, and `twitter:image`.
- **Anchors**: a fragment must name an element `id`, or an `<a name>`, on the
  target page. `#top` and text fragments (`#:~:text=`) always resolve.
- **Base path**: on a site served below `/<repo>/`, an absolute link that
  forgets the prefix is reported as `outside base`.
- **Deployment files** at the site root: version paths in Ardo's
  `versions.json`, and redirect and rewrite destinations in `_redirects`
  (Netlify, Cloudflare Pages) and `vercel.json`.

Links inside comments, scripts, styles, and other raw-text elements are
ignored, as a browser ignores them. External URLs are counted, not fetched.

## Install

The command-line tool:

```bash
cargo install --locked ferrolink
```

The development version, straight from the repository:

```bash
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/sebastian-software/ferrolink
```

For Node.js and Vite, without a Rust toolchain:

```bash
npm install --save-dev ferrolink
```

The npm package brings a prebuilt binary for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux
(arm64, x64; glibc and musl), and Windows (arm64, x64). It needs Node.js
20.19+ or 22.12+, as Vite 7 does.

## Usage

```bash
# A site served from the domain root
ferrolink check docs/build/client

# A GitHub Pages project site, served below /ardo/
ferrolink check docs/build/client --base /ardo/

# Absolute links to your own host (canonical, og:url) are checked too
ferrolink check dist --site-url https://example.org/docs/

# Keep checking links into an archived version, but not the links inside it
ferrolink check docs/build/pages --exclude 'v3/**'

# Accept links to versions that are deployed separately
ferrolink check docs/build/client --assume-present 'v[345]/**'

# Check links and assets, but not #fragments
ferrolink check dist --no-anchors

# Machine-readable output for CI annotations
ferrolink check dist --format json
```

The exit code is `0` when every reference resolves, `1` when issues were
found, and `2` when the check could not run.

`--exclude` skips the links *inside* matching pages; `--assume-present`
accepts links *to* matching paths, or to the `index.html` a host serves for
them, without looking for them in the build or checking their anchors. Both
take globs relative to the build directory. An `--assume-present` glob with a
leading `/` matches the absolute URL path instead, base path included, and so
also covers paths outside the base, such as `/blog/**` for another app on the
same host.

### Audit a static build for search

From a repository checkout, point the Rust CLI at the finished build and
give it the public site URL, including any deployment path.

```bash
cargo run --release --locked -- audit build/client --site-url https://example.org/ardo/ --format json
```

The audit reads `sitemap.xml`, `sitemap-index.xml`, or `sitemap_index.xml`
and follows local XML sitemap indexes. It reports malformed XML, invalid or
duplicate URLs, and targets absent from the build. When an entry contains
`lastmod`, it checks for a valid calendar date or a timestamp with a time zone.
For each HTML page in a sitemap, it checks for a matching canonical link
in the document head and detects `noindex` or `none` in `robots` and
`googlebot` meta tags. A page
marked `noindex` can stay in the build outside the sitemap. For sitemap HTML
pages without `noindex`, the audit requires one nonempty title in the head.
A meta description is optional. When present, it must contain text and appear
once in the head.

For pages with Open Graph metadata in the head, the audit checks that
`og:title`, `og:type`, `og:url`, and `og:image` are present and nonempty.
An optional `og:description` must contain text when declared. URLs must be
absolute HTTP(S) URLs. The audit compares `og:url` with the canonical when
the page has one valid canonical and checks that local `og:image` files exist.
Multiple image declarations are supported. See the [Open Graph protocol](https://ogp.me/).

The audit validates JSON syntax in embedded `application/ld+json` script
blocks throughout the built HTML. The `json_ld_syntax_invalid` finding
locates the parse error in the HTML file. Schema.org and rich-result checks
are tracked separately in the comparison below.

For HTML pages that declare `hreflang` alternates in the head, the audit
checks registered two-letter language codes, optional script and region
codes, and the optional `x-default` fallback. It requires absolute HTTP(S)
URLs and a self-reference. Local alternate targets must exist, and local
HTML targets must link back. URLs that resolve to the same built file count
as the same page. For alternates outside the deployment, only the declaration
is checked.

The audit also checks malformed or multiple canonical links and canonicals
that point to missing or non-indexable pages within this deployment. Relative
canonical links resolve against the page URL and its first `base href`, if
present.

At the origin root, the audit reads the build's `robots.txt` when present.
It discovers local sitemaps from `Sitemap:` declarations alongside the
conventional filenames. It reports malformed fields, invalid user-agent
tokens and rule paths, and rules before the first user-agent group.
Well-formed extension fields are accepted. It also reports sitemap URLs
blocked for Googlebot and points to the matching `Disallow` line. Sitemap
declarations for other origins or deployments are checked for URL syntax.

For a build deployed under a subpath, supply a local copy of the origin's
`/robots.txt` with `--robots`. The flag also lets you override the build file
for a site at the origin root.

```bash
cargo run --release --locked -- audit build/client --site-url https://example.org/ardo/ \
  --robots ./host-robots.txt --format json
```

To check internal reachability, pass `--check-reachability`. Ferrolink
starts at the site's home page and follows local `<a href>` and `<area href>`
links in the built HTML. A sitemap entry for an existing HTML page without
`noindex` produces `sitemap_unreachable` if the walk misses it. The same
option reports `sitemap_no_incoming_links` when no other built HTML page
links to the sitemap page. The site root and explicit entry points are
exempt from the incoming-link check. Both findings point to the sitemap entry.

Use the repeatable `--entry-point` option for separately linked sections.
Each entry is a public URL or an origin-relative path, including the
deployment prefix. Supplying an entry enables the check and can provide the
starting page for a build without a home page.

```bash
cargo run --release --locked -- audit build/client --site-url https://example.org/ardo/ \
  --check-reachability --entry-point /ardo/guide/ --format json
```

JSON output contains `summary` and an `issues` array. Each issue has a stable
`code`, a `source` path, a one-based `line` (zero for a missing element or
file), a nullable `url`, and a human-readable `message`. The `source` is
build-relative for build files and uses the supplied path for `--robots`. Use
the code for CI automation. Exit status is `0` for a clean audit, `1` for
findings, and `2` when the audit cannot run. The audit works offline against
the generated files.

### How URLs map to files

ferrolink follows the rules GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, and most
static servers share. A path ending in `/` serves its `index.html`. Otherwise
the exact file wins, then `<path>.html`, then `<path>/index.html`. Lookups are
case-sensitive, as on those hosts, even on a case-insensitive local disk.

## Node.js

```ts
import { check } from "ferrolink"

const report = await check({
  root: "dist",
  siteUrl: "https://example.org/docs/",
  exclude: ["v3/**"],
})
for (const issue of report.issues) {
  console.log(`${issue.source}:${issue.line} ${issue.kind} ${issue.href}`)
}
```

`check()` takes the options of the command line in camel case (`basePath`,
`siteUrl`, `exclude`, `assumePresent`, `anchors`, `deployFiles`, `threads`)
and resolves with the report `--format json` prints: `summary`, `issues`, and
`timings`. It runs on a worker thread, so the event loop stays free, and
rejects only when the check cannot run. Broken links are issues in the report.
`formatIssues(report.issues)` renders them the way the command line prints
them, grouped by file.

### Vite

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite"
import ferrolink from "ferrolink/vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [ferrolink({ siteUrl: "https://example.org/" })],
})
```

The plugin checks the client build output once the build is complete and
fails the build when it finds issues; `level: "warn"` logs them instead. It
takes the options of `check()` except `root`, plus `dir` to check another
directory than the client `build.outDir`. `basePath` defaults to Vite's
`base`. In an app build, where frameworks such as Ardo render their HTML in
`buildApp`, the check runs after every other `buildApp` hook, so it sees the
rendered pages. The plugin works with Vite 7 and 8.

### API stability

The JavaScript API is the supported way to use ferrolink from code. `check()`,
`formatIssues()`, the fields of the options and of the report, the issue kinds,
and the `ferrolink/vite` plugin with its options follow semantic versioning: before
1.0, a breaking change only comes with a new minor version (0.x.0) and is
called out in the changelog. New options, report fields, and issue kinds can
arrive in any minor version; treat an issue kind you do not know as an issue.
The values of `timings` and `origin`, error messages, and the text of log
output and of `formatIssues()` are not part of the contract. The Rust library API serves the CLI and the npm binding
and can change in any minor release before 1.0.

## Performance

On the 318-page Ardo documentation build (9.2 MB of HTML, 1,087 files), a full
check takes about 26 ms on an Apple M1 Ultra. The directory walk uses
[ferralk](https://github.com/sebastian-software/ferralk); pages are scanned on
every core.

ferrolink scans with [Ferroni](https://github.com/sebastian-software/ferroni)
regular expressions: one pattern finds comments and start tags, a second
splits the attributes of the tags that matter.
[docs/parsers.md](docs/parsers.md) records how it was chosen over the
html5gum, html5ever, and lol_html tokenizers on the same workload.

## Development

```bash
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --all-features --locked
cargo run --release -- check path/to/build
```

The npm package lives in `node/`, with the napi-rs binding in `node/native/`:

```bash
cd node
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm test
```

## Website development

The Ardo site in `homepage/` uses the shared Ferramenta theme: the Monografie
page system on the homepage and its reading layout on documentation
pages. The CLI reference, Node reference, parser decision and changelog are
generated from their canonical repository documents. Edit those sources, not
the generated routes.

```bash
cd homepage
pnpm install
pnpm dev
pnpm verify
```

Every specimen on the homepage is real output of the published npm package at
the version pinned in `homepage/package.json`; the parser chart reads the
tables in `docs/parsers.md`. `pnpm sample:write` regenerates
`app/data/home-samples.json`, and `pnpm verify` fails when it is stale, then
runs the source checks, the production build and browser checks at eight
widths. The built site is also checked by Ferrolink itself. GitHub Actions
deploys `main` to GitHub Pages.
